items.name: The Blair Witch Project
clues: Horror, filmed like a shaky home video. You hardly ever see what everyone is afraid of.
Three film students walk into a forest with their cameras to make a documentary. They never come back.
The marketing pretended it was all real: the students had really disappeared, and this was the film they left behind.
Long before most studios took the internet seriously, its website told the local legend as if it were true history.
‘Missing’ posters for the three actors went up, as if they were real missing people.
A witch from a small town called Blair, in the woods of Maryland.

items.name: Deadpool
clues: A superhero film, but rude, violent and very funny. Definitely not one for the children.
A man gets the power to heal from almost anything, but the experiment ruins his skin, and he wants revenge.
It came out just before Valentine’s Day 2016, so one billboard pretended it was a romantic film.
Another billboard had just three symbols: a skull, a pile of poo and the letter L.
The star wore the costume for months of jokes on TV and online, and once pretended to kill a TV presenter as an April Fool’s joke.
Ryan Reynolds in a red suit, a hero who never stops talking.

items.name: Smile
clues: Horror about a curse that passes from one person to the next.
A therapist keeps seeing people with a strange, frightening expression, and it seems to be following her.
The studio put the scary thing from the film into real life, where fans would see it by accident.
Clips from live TV spread fast online, and everyone asked: who are those people?
In September 2022, actors sat behind home plate at baseball games and stared into the TV cameras for innings at a time.
Its one-word title is what you do when you’re happy, but here it means something terrible.

items.name: Cloverfield
clues: A monster film, told entirely through one person’s handheld camera.
A going-away party in New York is interrupted when something huge attacks the city.
Before it came out, the marketing never showed you what the monster looked like.
Fans searched online for clues, and even a made-up Japanese drink got its own mysterious website.
In 2007 a teaser played in cinemas before Transformers with no title at all: just the producer’s name and a release date.
Produced by J.J. Abrams. In the trailer, the head of the Statue of Liberty crashes down a New York street.

items.name: Paranormal Activity
clues: Horror filmed with a home video camera, mostly at night, in one ordinary house.
A young couple put a camera in their bedroom to find out what is happening while they sleep.
It cost about $15,000 and was shot in the director’s own home, then a big studio bought it.
The studio asked fans to ‘demand’ it online. When enough people in a city asked, it opened there.
Its trailer showed the audience in the cinema, filmed with night vision, screaming and hiding their faces.
A word for ghostly, unexplained things, plus a word for things happening.

items.name: The Dark Knight
clues: A dark crime film and a superhero sequel. Many people still call it the best of its kind.
A criminal in clown make-up wants to prove that anyone in the city can become bad.
A huge game for fans ran for 15 months before the film came out, with over 11 million players in more than 75 countries.
Fans campaigned online for one of the film’s characters to win an election as the city’s top lawyer.
Players followed GPS clues to find mobile phones baked inside birthday cakes.
The Joker asks: ‘Why so serious?’, and Batman has to stop him.
